purpose: Per-tick and per-observation cost of the M05 scene before and after removing per-tick and per-save deep clones; informational, no FPS gate
machine: implementation container, 4 vCPU, Node 22.22.0, Rapier 0.21.0; one run each, ordinary run-to-run variance about +/-15%

workload.combat: seed 142, 2,400 ambient creatures, area 1, controller attacks/pulses toward the nearest enemy, 400 ticks
workload.idle: seed 142, no creatures, area 1 cleared, 300 settling ticks then 200 measured ticks

diagnosis: After every step PhysicsWorld built complete poses for every body (two structuredClone calls each) only to check finite values, and pose() deep-cloned recipes and memoized policies. M05's 84 props plus the terrain chunks they occupied multiplied that work; the browser adventure loop fell below real time (5 FPS) and its area could not clear in time.
fix: finite-state check reads Rapier values directly
pose() copies the recipe and policy structurally instead of structuredClone
only movable props occupy terrain chunks; fixed scenery never meets terrain colliders
stateHash covers raw Rapier bytes through the snapshot's checksum instead of serializing the byte array as JSON
poses and saves copy recipes, policies, body entries and ambient samples structurally (same keys and order as structuredClone, so JSON and hashes are unchanged; callers still own every object)
equivalence: npm run check passes 86/86 including save/replay/state-hash tests; terrain occupancy now differs by design, so pre-fix and final hashes are not comparable

browser.workload: Chromium 141 headless (software), 1440x1000, default 2,400 creatures, 'Begin the hunt' then the adventure e2e controller (observe() and input every 80 ms) for 20 s
browser.note: Most main-thread time in that test is its own observe() calls: each computes stateHash over a full save. The adventure loop clears only when simulated time keeps pace, so this harness cost decided the browser test.
